per_object_cap.stated: not applicable: the unit is a sandbox, not an object. Each command defaults to a 60-second timeout with a 30-minute hard cap.

retention.stated: Stopping keeps /workspace and resets everything else; 'you've got up to 7 days to start() it again before it's permanently deleted'. Only /workspace survives a stop, and failed sandboxes lose /workspace.

egress.terms: Not published. The overview page and the blog post state the compute and lifecycle meters and say nothing about a traffic allowance or a per-GB egress rate.

record.interface_detail: Python SDK ('Sandbox.create(plan="medium")') and an HTTP API, with a dashboard at deepinfra.com/dash/sandboxes.
record.tooling: The vendor's Python SDK and REST API; commands run inside the microVM and files move only through /workspace.
record.chaining: USD 0.054 an hour for the nano plan is USD 39.42 a month if never stopped, and a sandbox auto-stops after 24 hours of continuous running, so it is not an always-on machine. It belongs in the stack as a scratch executor next to earlier inference accounts, not as an answer to the cheap-VM questions.

limits.value: auto-stop after 24 continuous running hours, a default 1-hour idle timeout that cannot be disabled, and 7 days of stopped retention before deletion
25 non-stopped sandboxes per account; 'shared-fleet capacity can temporarily prevent creation'

record.limits_note: Billing runs while a sandbox is creating, starting, running or stopping, so 'per-second' includes boot and the disk save on stop. The plan shapes and rates are behind an authenticated catalog: GET /v1/sandboxes/catalog returned {"detail":"User is not authorized to access this resource"} to an unauthenticated request on 2026-10-24, and the docs say explicitly not to hardcode the numbers.
record.binding_note: The 24-hour auto-stop is the first hard wall: no configuration on the pages read lifts it, so the machine cannot be an always-on monitor or VPN node even before the price matters.

identity_cost.detail: A DeepInfra account is required and sandboxes draw on DeepInfra billing; the catalog endpoint refuses an unauthenticated caller, so plan shapes and prices are visible only to a signed-in account. Card types, any authorisation hold, and whether a debit or prepaid card is accepted were not established.

record.reliability_note: Two documented loss paths: a failed sandbox loses /workspace, and everything outside /workspace is discarded on stop. Shared-fleet capacity can refuse creation.
record.confidence_note: The nano rate, the per-second meter and the whole lifecycle are quoted from DeepInfra's own blog and docs, read. The rate-to-shape mapping is not documented publicly: the vendor directs readers to an authenticated catalog, so the shape fields stay null rather than guessed. What would raise it: a signed-in read of /v1/sandboxes/catalog, which would give the exact vCPU/RAM/disk of the nano plan.

evidence.proved: quoted: 'the `nano` plan starts at just $0.054/hour, billed by the second' and 'Leave one running and it auto-stops after 24 hours'
retention: 'Stopping just pauses it: /workspace sticks around, everything else resets to a clean image. From there you've got up to 7 days to start() it again before it's permanently deleted.'
billing: 'Billing is per-second with no minimum, and only runs while a sandbox is creating, starting, running, or stopping - a stopped sandbox costs nothing'
no public shape/rate table: 'For current plan specs (vCPU, RAM, disk) and hourly pricing, don't hardcode numbers - check the live catalog'

record.notes: Arithmetic: USD 0.054 an hour × 730 = USD 39.42 a month if the auto-stop did not exist; × 300 h = USD 16.20. The auto-stop makes the 730-hour figure hypothetical, and it is recorded as the price of the meter rather than the price of a machine. What the nano shape actually contains is unverified because the catalog is authenticated.

extras.price_arithmetic: 0.054/hr × 730 h = USD 39.42; × 300 h = USD 16.20. Both assume the sandbox is never auto-stopped, which the vendor's 24-hour rule makes impossible in practice.

record.notes: 50,000,000,000 tokens / 1,000,000 = 50,000 units of a million tokens; 50,000 x USD 0.06 = USD 3,000 input-equivalent; 50,000 x USD 0.18 = USD 9,000 output-equivalent. A third-party list circulating on 2026-10-22 states the grant is 1,000,000,000 tokens, which the vendor page contradicts by a factor of 50; the vendor figure is recorded. This is the largest per-entity inference credit found among evaluated providers and it is closed to a person without a funded company. It is a separate programme from the signup record above: the same provider carries both a closed grant and a card-gated API.
